question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(a), if the Commission finds a broker, qualifying broker, or associate broker violated the license law, what unusual sanction option -- distinct from suspension or revocation -- may it impose?
choice_a: Revoke the broker's license and simultaneously issue that person a salesperson's license
choice_b: Permanently bar the person from any future real estate involvement
choice_c: Automatically transfer the person's listings to another firm
choice_d: Require the person to co-sign all future contracts with a supervising attorney
explanation: Among the Commission's sanction options under 43-40-25(a) is revoking a broker's, qualifying broker's, or associate broker's license while simultaneously issuing that same person a salesperson's license, effectively demoting rather than fully ousting the licensee.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(a), besides fines and license actions, what financial burden may the Commission impose on a sanctioned licensee?
choice_a: Monetary assessments to reimburse the Commission for its administrative, investigative, and legal costs
choice_b: A mandatory donation to the Real Estate Education, Research, and Recovery Fund equal to one year's commissions
choice_c: Payment of the complaining party's attorney's fees in all cases
choice_d: Reimbursement of the competing broker's lost commission
explanation: 43-40-25(a) authorizes the Commission to impose monetary assessments necessary to reimburse it for the administrative, investigative, and legal costs incurred in a disciplinary matter, separate from any fine.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, what is the General Assembly's stated purpose for authorizing citations and letters of findings?
choice_a: To give the Commission measures to use as alternatives to the sanctions otherwise provided for in Code Section 43-40-25
choice_b: To replace the formal sanction process entirely for all future violations
choice_c: To shift disciplinary authority from the Commission to the courts
choice_d: To require every violation to be handled through criminal prosecution
explanation: 43-40-25.2 exists to give the Commission alternative measures -- citations and letters of findings -- to use instead of the sanctions otherwise available under 43-40-25, not to displace that section entirely.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, how is a citation or letter of findings legally characterized?
choice_a: It is not construed as a disciplinary sanction
choice_b: It is automatically treated as equivalent to license revocation
choice_c: It is a criminal conviction for licensing purposes
choice_d: It permanently bars the licensee from Commission office
explanation: The statute expressly provides that a citation and letter of findings are not to be construed as a disciplinary sanction, distinguishing this alternative track from the formal sanctions enumerated in 43-40-25.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, how may a citation be served on a licensee, and what must it inform the licensee of?
choice_a: Personally or by mail, and it must give notice of the alleged violations and the opportunity to request a contested case hearing under Chapter 13 of Title 50
choice_b: Only by personal service from a sheriff's deputy, with no hearing rights
choice_c: Only by publication in a newspaper of general circulation
choice_d: Only by certified mail, and it waives all hearing rights automatically
explanation: A citation may be served personally or by mail and must give the licensee notice of the alleged violations plus the opportunity to request a contested case hearing under the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 13 of Title 50).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who makes, prints, or circulates a notice or advertisement for a property that indicates a preference or limitation based on a protected characteristic has committed:
choice_a: A statutory unfair trade practice, separate from the Commission's own fair housing rule
choice_b: No violation, since only the newspaper publishing the ad is liable
choice_c: A violation only if the ad is published outside Georgia
choice_d: A minor infraction correctable only by a private lawsuit, not Commission discipline
explanation: Discriminatory advertising is listed among the unfair trade practices in O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b) itself -- a statutory ground for discipline that exists alongside (not instead of) the Commission's Rule 520-1-.13 fair housing provisions.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), falsely telling an interested buyer that a listed property is 'no longer available' when it is, in order to steer them elsewhere, is an unfair trade practice known as:
choice_a: Misrepresenting the availability of property for inspection or sale
choice_b: A legitimate negotiation tactic if done to protect the seller's interests
choice_c: Permitted so long as the licensee later corrects the record in writing
choice_d: Only a violation if the buyer can prove financial loss
explanation: Misrepresenting whether a property is available for inspection or sale is separately enumerated as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), regardless of the licensee's underlying motive.

question: How does 'steering' differ from 'blockbusting' as prohibited practices under Georgia real estate law?
choice_a: Steering channels buyers toward or away from neighborhoods based on protected characteristics, while blockbusting involves representing that a protected class's presence will cause value decline or other harm to induce a transaction
choice_b: They are the same practice under two different names with no meaningful distinction
choice_c: Steering only applies to rental housing, while blockbusting only applies to sales
choice_d: Steering is a federal-only violation with no Georgia counterpart
explanation: Both are prohibited, but they are distinct practices: steering directs prospective buyers or renters toward or away from particular areas based on a protected characteristic, while blockbusting specifically involves inducing panic-selling or transactions by representing that a protected class's presence will harm property values, safety, or schools.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), advertising material that is 'misleading or inaccurate' -- even where no protected class is involved -- is:
choice_a: A separately enumerated unfair trade practice on its own
choice_b: Permitted as ordinary marketing puffery in all cases
choice_c: Only actionable if a competitor, not a consumer, complains
choice_d: Regulated exclusively by the Federal Trade Commission, not GREC
explanation: Beyond discriminatory advertising, general misleading or inaccurate advertising material is its own separately listed unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), independent of any fair housing violation.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who receives earnest money from a buyer and fails to account for it to the principals entitled to it has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for failure to account for money belonging to others
choice_b: No violation as long as the money is eventually located
choice_c: A violation only if the amount exceeds $10,000
choice_d: A matter solely for the buyer's civil attorney, outside Commission jurisdiction
explanation: Failing to account for money or other property belonging to a principal is independently listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), regardless of whether the funds are eventually recovered.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), depositing a principal's earnest money into the licensee's personal operating account alongside the licensee's own funds constitutes:
choice_a: Commingling, an unfair trade practice
choice_b: A permitted bookkeeping shortcut for sole proprietors
choice_c: A violation only if the licensee later spends the funds
choice_d: Acceptable if the licensee documents the deposit in a spreadsheet
explanation: Commingling the money or other property of a licensee's principals with the licensee's own funds is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), independent of whether the funds are ultimately misused.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a salesperson who accepts a commission on a transaction from someone other than the broker under whom the salesperson is affiliated (without proper authorization) has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for accepting compensation from an unauthorized source
choice_b: No violation, since salespersons may accept payment from any party to the deal
choice_c: A violation only if the amount exceeds the broker's usual commission split
choice_d: A tax matter only, outside Commission jurisdiction
explanation: Accepting a commission, rebate, or other compensation from a source other than the licensee's own employing/qualifying broker, without proper authorization, is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who secretly buys a listed property through a shell entity while still acting as the seller's agent -- without disclosing the licensee's own interest -- has committed:
choice_a: Acting in the dual capacity of agent and undisclosed principal, an unfair trade practice
choice_b: A permitted investment strategy so long as fair market value is paid
choice_c: A violation only if the seller later complains
choice_d: A matter regulated only by the entity's operating agreement
explanation: Acting in the dual capacity of agent and undisclosed principal in the same transaction is separately listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b) -- distinct from Rule 520-1-.11's disclosure-to-broker requirement, this statutory ground focuses on non-disclosure of the licensee's own principal interest.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), telling a buyer 'this property will definitely be worth 20% more within a year if you buy now' as a guarantee to induce the sale is:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for guaranteeing future profits
choice_b: Permitted opinion testimony protected as free speech
choice_c: Only prohibited if made in a written advertisement
choice_d: A violation only if the market later declines
explanation: Guaranteeing or authorizing a guarantee of future profits resulting from the resale of property is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), regardless of whether the market ultimately moves as predicted.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who places a 'For Sale' sign on a property without the written consent of the owner has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for unauthorized signage
choice_b: No violation, since signage is purely a marketing decision for the licensee
choice_c: A violation only if a neighbor complains to a homeowners' association
choice_d: A zoning matter handled solely by the local municipality
explanation: Placing a sign on any property offering it for sale or rent without the written consent of the owner is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), advertising or offering a property for sale without the knowledge and authorization of the owner (or the owner's authorized agent) is:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice
choice_b: Permitted if the licensee believes in good faith the owner would want to sell
choice_c: Only a violation if the property is ultimately sold to a third party
choice_d: A civil trespass matter unrelated to licensing
explanation: Offering real property for sale, lease, or rent without the knowledge and consent of the owner or the owner's authorized agent is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who persuades a party to break an existing brokerage or purchase contract with another licensee, for the purpose of substituting a new contract with the first licensee, has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for inducing a breach of contract
choice_b: A permitted competitive business practice
choice_c: A violation only if the original contract was exclusive
choice_d: A matter solely between the two competing brokers, outside Commission jurisdiction
explanation: Inducing any party to a contract to break that contract for the purpose of substituting a new contract in which the inducing licensee is a beneficiary is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee (not a certified or licensed appraiser) who tells a lender their comparative market analysis is an 'appraisal' of the property's value has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for misrepresenting an opinion of value as an appraisal without appraiser credentials
choice_b: No violation, since real estate licensees are automatically qualified to appraise property
choice_c: A violation only if the lender relies on the number to fund the loan
choice_d: A matter regulated solely by the Georgia Real Estate Appraisers Board, not GREC
explanation: Misrepresenting an opinion of value as an 'appraisal' without holding an appropriate appraiser license or certification is an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b) -- a CMA is not an appraisal, and calling it one to a lender or party misleads them about its reliability and legal standing.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a Georgia-licensed salesperson who brokers a real estate transaction in another state without holding a license valid there has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for unlicensed activity in another jurisdiction
choice_b: No violation, since a Georgia license is automatically recognized nationwide
choice_c: A violation only if the other state files a formal complaint with GREC
choice_d: A matter entirely outside GREC's authority since the conduct occurred elsewhere
explanation: Engaging in real estate brokerage activity in another state or jurisdiction without holding a license valid there is listed as an unfair trade practice under Georgia's 43-40-25(b), even though the underlying conduct occurred outside Georgia.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a broker who pays a 'finder's fee' commission to an unlicensed individual for referring a buyer has, absent a narrow statutory exception, committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for paying compensation to an unlicensed person
choice_b: A permitted practice as long as the fee is disclosed to the buyer
choice_c: A violation only if the unlicensed person actively negotiated the deal
choice_d: A matter governed solely by IRS 1099 reporting rules
explanation: Paying a commission or valuable consideration to a person not licensed as a broker or salesperson, outside the chapter's narrow exceptions, is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a written listing agreement that never states a definite expiration date is:
choice_a: Grounds for an unfair trade practice violation
choice_b: Standard industry practice with no legal significance
choice_c: A violation only if the listing runs longer than one year
choice_d: Only a concern for commercial listings, not residential
explanation: Failing to include a definite expiration date in a written listing (or other brokerage engagement) is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b) -- an open-ended listing with no fixed end date is itself a violation.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), failing to promptly deliver a copy of a signed purchase agreement or offer to the parties involved is:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice
choice_b: Permitted so long as the original is kept safely in the broker's file
choice_c: Only a problem if the deal later falls through
choice_d: A courtesy, not a legal obligation
explanation: Failure to timely furnish a copy of a purchase agreement, offer, or other transaction document to the parties involved is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), reinforcing the parties' right to their own signed paperwork.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), failing to furnish a party to a closed transaction with an accurate closing statement in a timely manner is:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice
choice_b: A violation only if the party is the buyer, not the seller
choice_c: Solely the closing attorney's responsibility, never the licensee's
choice_d: Only a concern in cash transactions with no lender involved
explanation: Failing to timely furnish an accurate closing statement to a party to the transaction is separately listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b).

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee representing both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction without both parties' written consent has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for undisclosed dual representation
choice_b: No violation, since Georgia does not regulate dual agency
choice_c: A violation only if one party later claims to have been harmed financially
choice_d: A matter governed exclusively by the MLS rules, not state law
explanation: Acting for more than one party in a transaction without the written consent of all parties is listed as a distinct unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), separate from the undisclosed-principal provision.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a salesperson who collects an earnest money check from a buyer and sits on it for two weeks before turning it in to the broker has likely committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for failing to promptly account for and deliver funds received to the licensee's broker
choice_b: No violation, since the salesperson eventually delivered the check
choice_c: A violation only if the check bounces
choice_d: A matter solely between the salesperson and the buyer
explanation: A salesperson or associate broker's failure to promptly account for and remit funds received on behalf of a principal to their broker is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), regardless of whether the funds are eventually delivered.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee who files a document against a property's title to pressure a seller into paying a disputed commission, despite having no valid legal claim, has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for clouding title without a valid claim
choice_b: A legitimate self-help remedy for unpaid commissions
choice_c: A violation only if a court later voids the filing
choice_d: A matter regulated only by the county clerk's recording office
explanation: Filing a lien, lis pendens, or similar document to cloud title without a good faith, valid legal claim is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), preventing licensees from weaponizing the recording system in fee disputes.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a general pattern of demonstrated incompetence or dishonest dealing by a licensee is:
choice_a: Itself a separately enumerated unfair trade practice, even without a more specific violation applying
choice_b: Not actionable unless it fits one of the other, more specific enumerated categories
choice_c: Only relevant to the initial licensing exam, not post-licensure conduct
choice_d: A basis for civil liability only, never Commission discipline
explanation: 43-40-25(b) includes a broad catch-all ground covering demonstrated incompetency or dishonest dealing, allowing the Commission to act even when conduct doesn't fit neatly into one of the more specific enumerated practices.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), a licensee holding only a Community Association Manager (CAM) license who performs general brokerage acts beyond the scope of CAM licensure has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for exceeding the scope of the CAM license
choice_b: No violation, since a CAM license is functionally identical to a broker's license
choice_c: A violation only if a homeowner files a written complaint
choice_d: A matter regulated solely by the community association's board
explanation: 43-40-25(b) addresses a CAM licensee performing brokerage acts beyond the scope of that more limited license as an unfair trade practice -- a CAM license does not carry full brokerage authority.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25(b), when a property management agreement terminates, a licensee who fails to deliver the owner's funds and records within the required time frame has committed:
choice_a: An unfair trade practice for failure to timely deliver funds and records upon termination of a management agreement
choice_b: No violation, since the licensee's fiduciary duty ends the moment the agreement terminates
choice_c: A violation only if the owner sues in small claims court first
choice_d: A matter governed exclusively by the terms of the management agreement, never by statute
explanation: Failing to timely deliver an owner's funds and records upon termination of a management agreement is listed as an unfair trade practice under 43-40-25(b), reflecting the licensee's continuing duty to wind up the relationship properly.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.1, may a licensee complete a listing, sales, or lease contract using an attorney-prepared preprinted form without that constituting the unauthorized practice of law?
choice_a: Yes, but this authorization does not extend to preparing a deed or conducting a real estate closing
choice_b: No, only a licensed attorney may fill in any real estate contract form
choice_c: Yes, and this also authorizes licensees to prepare deeds and conduct closings
choice_d: Only if the licensee has a paralegal certificate
explanation: 43-40-25.1 permits licensees to complete contract forms prepared by an attorney (listing, sales, lease, etc.) without that being the unauthorized practice of law, but this narrow authorization does not extend to deed preparation or conducting a closing -- both of which remain attorney-only functions in Georgia.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-27(a), Commission investigations of licensee conduct are generally limited to what look-back period, and what are the exceptions?
choice_a: Generally limited to conduct within the prior 3 years, with exceptions for fraud, breach of fiduciary duty involving funds, and matters already in pending litigation
choice_b: Unlimited -- there is no time restriction on any investigation
choice_c: Generally limited to 6 months, with no exceptions
choice_d: Generally limited to 10 years, matching the broker felony look-back period
explanation: 43-40-27(a) generally restricts Commission investigations to conduct occurring within the prior three years, but carves out exceptions for fraud, breach of fiduciary duty involving funds, and conduct already the subject of pending litigation.

question: Under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 520-1-.06(1)(c), how does Georgia treat 'net listings' -- where a broker's compensation is any amount above a set minimum the seller will accept?
choice_a: They are categorically prohibited, not merely discouraged
choice_b: They are permitted with the seller's written informed consent
choice_c: They are permitted only for commercial property
choice_d: They are permitted but must be capped at 10% of the sale price
explanation: Georgia categorically prohibits net listing arrangements under Rule 520-1-.06(1)(c) -- unlike some states that merely discourage or heavily regulate them, Georgia bars the practice outright regardless of seller consent.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-201, how is 'familial status' defined for purposes of Georgia's fair housing protections?
choice_a: Relating to one or more individuals under 18 domiciled with a parent/guardian, a pregnant person, or a person in the process of securing legal custody of a minor
choice_b: Relating only to married couples with biological children
choice_c: Relating only to households with more than four occupants
choice_d: Relating only to single-parent households
explanation: Georgia's fair housing definitions section covers a person's status of having a child under 18 living with them, being pregnant, or being in the process of securing legal custody of a minor -- mirroring the federal Fair Housing Act's familial status protection added in 1988.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-202, a housing provider's refusal to permit a tenant with a disability to make reasonable modifications to their dwelling, at the tenant's own expense, is:
choice_a: A discriminatory housing practice, since disabled tenants must generally be permitted reasonable modifications
choice_b: Always permitted, since the provider owns the property
choice_c: Only unlawful if the modification is free of charge to the tenant
choice_d: A matter left entirely to lease terms, unregulated by fair housing law
explanation: Georgia's fair housing law requires that persons with disabilities generally be permitted to make reasonable modifications to a dwelling at their own expense; refusing to allow this is a discriminatory housing practice, mirroring the federal Fair Housing Act's disability provisions.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-202, newly constructed multifamily dwellings with a required number of units must include what feature for persons with disabilities?
choice_a: Accessible design and construction features
choice_b: No specific design requirement -- accessibility is purely voluntary
choice_c: A requirement that applies only to government-subsidized housing
choice_d: A requirement limited to buildings over 10 stories
explanation: Georgia's fair housing law requires covered new multifamily construction to include accessible design and construction features for persons with disabilities, paralleling the federal Fair Housing Act's design-and-construction requirements.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-203, discriminating against a person based on a protected characteristic in access to or membership in a real estate-related organization (such as an MLS) is:
choice_a: A discriminatory practice separately prohibited by Georgia's fair housing law
choice_b: Permitted, since private organizations may set their own membership criteria
choice_c: Only prohibited for statewide organizations, not local boards
choice_d: Regulated solely by the organization's private bylaws
explanation: O.C.G.A. 8-3-203 separately prohibits discrimination based on protected characteristics in access to or membership/participation in real estate-related organizations, such as multiple listing services and real estate boards.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-204, discriminating against a protected class in the terms of real estate-related financing, lending, or appraisal services -- commonly known as 'redlining' -- is:
choice_a: A discriminatory housing practice prohibited under Georgia's fair housing law
choice_b: Regulated only by federal banking law, not Georgia state law
choice_c: Permitted if the lender applies the same criteria to all applicants of a given credit score
choice_d: Prohibited only for government-backed loans
explanation: O.C.G.A. 8-3-204 prohibits discrimination in the availability or terms of real estate-related financing, lending, and appraisal services based on protected characteristics -- the practice historically known as redlining.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-205, which of the following is a recognized exemption from Georgia's fair housing law?
choice_a: A bona fide religious organization may limit occupancy or give preference to its own members in housing it owns or operates for non-commercial purposes
choice_b: Any landlord may refuse to rent to families with children under any circumstances
choice_c: Real estate licensees are exempt from fair housing law entirely
choice_d: Discrimination is permitted for any property listed for under $100,000
explanation: Georgia's fair housing law, like the federal Fair Housing Act, exempts certain non-commercial housing operated by religious organizations that limit occupancy or give preference to their own members, along with a similarly limited private club exemption.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-205, 'housing for older persons' meeting specific statutory criteria (commonly 55-and-over communities) may be exempt from which protected category?
choice_a: Familial status
choice_b: Race
choice_c: National origin
choice_d: Religion
explanation: Qualifying housing for older persons -- meeting specific occupancy and verification criteria -- may lawfully exclude families with children under the familial status exemption; this exemption does not extend to race, national origin, religion, or any other protected class.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-206, who is charged with enforcing Georgia's fair housing law through investigation and conciliation of complaints?
choice_a: The administrator of the Georgia Commission on Equal Opportunity
choice_b: The Georgia Real Estate Commission exclusively
choice_c: The county sheriff's office where the property is located
choice_d: The Georgia Secretary of State
explanation: Georgia's fair housing law is enforced through the administrator of the Georgia Commission on Equal Opportunity, who investigates complaints and pursues conciliation -- a separate enforcement track from GREC's own licensee-discipline authority under Rule 520-1-.13.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 8-3-222, coercing, intimidating, threatening, or interfering with a person who has exercised a right protected by Georgia's fair housing law is:
choice_a: A separately prohibited act, distinct from the underlying discriminatory housing practice itself
choice_b: Only unlawful if it also independently qualifies as assault under criminal law
choice_c: Permitted as long as no physical contact occurs
choice_d: Only prohibited if committed by a licensee, not a private individual
explanation: O.C.G.A. 8-3-222 separately prohibits coercion, intimidation, threats, or interference against anyone exercising a fair housing right (or assisting another in doing so) -- an anti-retaliation provision independent of the underlying discrimination claim.

question: The federal Fair Housing Act was originally enacted as Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968; the 1988 Fair Housing Amendments Act added which two protected classes to the original list?
choice_a: Familial status and disability (handicap)
choice_b: Sex and religion
choice_c: Age and marital status
choice_d: Sexual orientation and gender identity
explanation: The original 1968 Act protected race, color, religion, sex, and national origin; the 1988 Fair Housing Amendments Act added familial status and disability (handicap), bringing the total to the seven classes now recognized federally and mirrored in Georgia's own fair housing law.
source_note: hedge: standard federal Fair Housing Act history, not GA-specific

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, a person who believes they experienced housing discrimination generally has how long to file an administrative complaint with HUD?
choice_a: One year from the alleged discriminatory act
choice_b: 30 days from the alleged discriminatory act
choice_c: Five years from the alleged discriminatory act
choice_d: There is no time limit for a HUD administrative complaint
explanation: A HUD administrative fair housing complaint generally must be filed within one year of the alleged discriminatory housing practice; a private federal civil suit has a separate, longer two-year limitations period.
source_note: hedge: standard federal Fair Housing Act procedural fact, not GA-specific

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, a private civil lawsuit alleging housing discrimination generally must be filed within how long of the discriminatory act?
choice_a: Two years
choice_b: 90 days
choice_c: Six months
choice_d: Ten years
explanation: A private federal civil action under the Fair Housing Act generally must be filed within two years of the discriminatory housing practice, distinct from the shorter one-year window for filing a HUD administrative complaint.
source_note: hedge: standard federal Fair Housing Act procedural fact, not GA-specific

question: The federal Fair Housing Act's limited exemption for an owner-occupied dwelling of no more than four units where the owner lives in one unit (commonly called the 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption) allows the owner to do what, subject to conditions?
choice_a: Choose tenants without regard to most fair housing protected classes, but the exemption does not permit discriminatory advertising and does not apply if a real estate licensee is used
choice_b: Discriminate freely with no conditions whatsoever, including using discriminatory advertising
choice_c: Discriminate only based on race, which remains fully exempt under all circumstances
choice_d: Apply only to commercial rental properties, never residential
explanation: The federal owner-occupied small-building exemption is narrow: it does not authorize discriminatory advertising, and it is unavailable if a real estate licensee or agent is used in the rental -- a licensee involved in such a transaction cannot rely on the owner's exemption to discriminate.
source_note: hedge: standard federal Fair Housing Act exemption, not GA-specific

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act's limited exemption for a private individual owner selling or renting a single-family home without using a real estate licensee, how many such sales may the owner make within a 24-month period and still claim the exemption?
choice_a: No more than three
choice_b: Unlimited, as long as no licensee is used
choice_c: Exactly one
choice_d: Ten
explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act's private-individual single-family-home exemption is capped at no more than three such sales in any 24-month period, does not permit discriminatory advertising, and is unavailable once the owner uses a real estate licensee.
source_note: hedge: standard federal Fair Housing Act exemption, not GA-specific

question: Under fair housing reasonable-accommodation principles, a housing provider's blanket 'no pets' policy generally must yield to what kind of animal for a tenant with a disability-related need?
choice_a: A service or assistance/emotional support animal, which is treated as a reasonable accommodation rather than a 'pet'
choice_b: No exception exists -- 'no pets' policies are always fully enforceable
choice_c: Only animals under 10 pounds qualify for any accommodation
choice_d: The provider may charge a standard pet deposit for a qualifying assistance animal, just as for any pet
explanation: A service or assistance/emotional support animal needed because of a disability is treated as a reasonable accommodation, not a 'pet' -- a provider generally cannot apply pet bans, breed/weight restrictions, or standard pet fees/deposits to a qualifying assistance animal.
source_note: hedge: standard federal Fair Housing Act reasonable-accommodation principle, not GA-specific

question: Under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(a) (BRRETA), what standard of duty does a Georgia broker owe a client or customer, absent a written agreement to the contrary?
choice_a: Only the statutory duties set out in BRRETA, exercised with reasonable care -- not a common-law fiduciary duty
choice_b: A full common-law fiduciary duty identical to that of a trustee
choice_c: No duty at all unless a lawsuit is filed
choice_d: A duty owed only to clients, never to customers
explanation: BRRETA displaces the common-law fiduciary standard by default: a Georgia broker owes only the duties and obligations set out in the Act, performed with reasonable care, unless the parties expressly agree in a signed writing to something more -- a distinctive feature of Georgia agency law.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-4(b) (BRRETA), if a broker already has a brokerage relationship with one party and then enters a new brokerage relationship involving the same transaction, what must the broker do?
choice_a: Timely disclose that fact and the new brokerage relationship to all brokers, customers, or clients involved in the contemplated transaction
choice_b: Nothing -- disclosure is only required if a party specifically asks
choice_c: Terminate the earlier relationship immediately and automatically
choice_d: Obtain a court order before proceeding
explanation: BRRETA requires a broker who enters a new brokerage relationship while an existing one is in place (regarding the same contemplated transaction) to timely disclose both the existing relationship and the new one to all brokers, customers, and clients involved.

question: Under BRRETA, is 'dual agency' -- one broker representing both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction -- permitted in Georgia?
choice_a: Yes, expressly permitted under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12, provided the required written consent is obtained with the statutorily specified content
choice_b: No, dual agency is categorically prohibited in Georgia
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial transactions, never residential
choice_d: It is permitted only with verbal consent from both parties
explanation: O.C.G.A. 10-6A-12 expressly permits dual agency in Georgia, but requires written consent from the parties containing the content specified by statute -- Georgia does not ban dual agency outright, unlike some states.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 10-6A-13 (BRRETA), in a 'designated agency' arrangement, to whom does each individually designated agent owe the full statutory brokerage duties?
choice_a: Only to that agent's own client, not to the other party's designated agent's client
choice_b: Equally to both the buyer and the seller at all times
choice_c: Only to the qualifying broker of the firm, not to either party
choice_d: To whichever party pays the commission
explanation: BRRETA's designated agency provision allows a firm to designate different affiliated licensees to represent the buyer and seller separately within the same firm; each designated agent owes the full statutory duties only to their own designated client, not to the other party.
